01.note: The people of Beit She'an had a custom of not traveling from Tyre to the market in Sidon on Friday, the eve of Shabbat. Their children came to Rabbi Yohanan and asked to be released from it: their fathers could afford to stay home, they said, but they could not. Rabbi Yohanan told them their fathers had already accepted the custom upon themselves, and quoted Proverbs: "My son, hear your father's rebuke and do not abandon your mother's teaching."
01.why: The mishna is discussing the duty to keep local customs; this case shows that a custom taken on by one generation binds the next, even when it has become a hardship.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage the children of Beit She'an asked to cancel their fathers' custom; he refused.

terms.meaning: Friday, the day before the Sabbath, when people prepare food and the house for the day of rest.

02.note: Yehuda and Hillel, the sons of Rabban Gamliel, bathed together in the city of Kabul, where the custom was that brothers did not bathe together. The whole city denounced them, saying they had never seen such a thing in all their days. Hillel slipped away to the outer chamber rather than tell the townspeople that what they had done was permitted.
02.why: Rav Hisda limited the rule against permitting local stringencies to Samaritans; the Gemara cites this incident to challenge him, since here the Sages refused to permit something even before ordinary Jews.

people.name: Yehuda
people.about: A son of Rabban Gamliel, who bathed with his brother in Kabul.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A son of Rabban Gamliel; when the city objected, he left rather than tell them it was allowed.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Father of Yehuda and Hillel.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara as an authority.
A group living in the Land of Israel who kept some Jewish practices; the Sages did not trust them to keep a leniency within its limits.

03.note: In the city of Birei the custom was not to go out on Shabbat wearing wide, slipper-like shoes. Yehuda and Hillel, the sons of Rabban Gamliel, went out in such shoes there, and the city denounced them, saying they had never seen such a thing. The brothers took the shoes off and gave them to their servants, and did not want to tell the people that it was permitted.
03.why: This is the second of three incidents the Gemara brings to challenge Rav Hisda's claim that one may not permit a local stringency only before Samaritans; the Gemara later answers that townspeople without Sages among them are treated like Samaritans.

people.name: Yehuda
people.about: A son of Rabban Gamliel, who wore wide shoes on Shabbat in Birei.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: A son of Rabban Gamliel, who wore wide shoes on Shabbat in Birei.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Father of Yehuda and Hillel.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which carrying objects in public areas is forbidden.

04.note: In Akko the custom was not to sit on gentiles' stools on Shabbat. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel sat on such stools there on Shabbat, and the whole city denounced him, saying they had never seen such a thing. He moved down onto the ground and did not want to tell them that it was permitted.
04.why: This is the last of three incidents raised against Rav Hisda; the Gemara answers that people in such towns, where Sages are not found, have the status of Samaritans, so one may not permit their stringencies before them.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who sat on gentiles' stools in Akko and moved to the ground when the city objected.

terms.meaning: Benches non-Jews used for displaying merchandise; sitting on them on Shabbat could look like doing business.
A group the Sages did not trust to keep a leniency within its limits; the Gemara likens townspeople without Sages to them.

05.note: When Rabba bar bar Hana came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia, he ate a kind of stomach fat that was eaten in the Land of Israel but avoided in Babylonia. Rav Avira the Elder and Rabba, son of Rav Huna, came in to see him, and when he saw them he hid what he was eating. They went and told Abaye, who said to them: he has made you into Samaritans.
05.why: The Gemara has just said that one may not permit a local stringency in front of Samaritans or people like them; Abaye reads Rabba bar bar Hana's hiding the food as treating the two Sages that way. The Gemara then asks how he could eat it at all.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and kept eating fat the Babylonians avoided.

people.name: Rav Avira the Elder
people.about: A Sage who visited Rabba bar bar Hana and saw him hide his food.

people.name: Rabba, son of Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who visited Rabba bar bar Hana with Rav Avira.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage the two visitors told; he said Rabba bar bar Hana had treated them as Samaritans.

terms.meaning: A group the Sages did not trust to keep a leniency within its limits, so permitted things were hidden from them rather than explained.

06.note: Rabba bar bar Hana reports what Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar told him. Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar once followed Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya into a garden, where the older Sage took cabbage that had grown on its own in the Sabbatical Year, ate some and gave him some. He told him: in my presence you may eat this, but not when I am absent. I saw Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai eat it, so I may rely on him; you did not see him, so eat it only when you are with me.
06.why: Rabba bar bar Hana had just told his son never to eat a disputed fat, even in his presence; the Gemara notes that by relating this story he contradicts himself, since here a student may eat in his teacher's presence.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The Sage who passes on this account.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar
people.about: The student who followed his teacher into the garden and was given the cabbage.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya
people.about: The Sage who ate the cabbage and told his student when he could eat it.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: The Sage whom Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya had seen eat such cabbage.

terms.meaning: Plants that sprout on their own in a field without being sown.
Every seventh year, when the Torah forbids working the land in the Land of Israel; the Sages also forbade most crops that grew on their own.

07.note: Rav Natan bar Asya traveled from Rav's study hall to Pumbedita on the second day of the festival of Shavuot, a day kept as a festival in the Diaspora. Rav Yosef excommunicated him. Abaye asked why he did not flog him instead, and Rav Yosef answered that he had done worse to him, since in the Land of Israel they vote to flog a Torah scholar but not to excommunicate him. Another version says Rav Yosef flogged him; Abaye asked why he did not excommunicate him, and Rav Yosef said that for a Torah scholar he had done what was best for him, since flogging is the lighter punishment.
07.why: The Gemara has just ruled that labor on the second festival day of the Diaspora is forbidden in a settled area, even by those who know the calendar; this incident shows a Sage being punished for breaking that day by traveling.

people.name: Rav Natan bar Asya
people.about: A Torah scholar who traveled to Pumbedita on the second festival day of Shavuot and was punished for it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who punished Rav Natan bar Asya.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Questioned Rav Yosef's choice of punishment in both versions.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose study hall Rav Natan left; with Shmuel he rules that one excommunicates for breaking the second festival day.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who, with Rav, rules that one excommunicates for breaking the second festival day of the Diaspora.

terms.meaning: Outside the Land of Israel each festival is kept for an extra day, a custom from when the Diaspora could not be sure which day the new month began.
Placed under a ban by a court: the person is shunned by the community until the ban is lifted.
A name the Sages use for Shavuot, the festival seven weeks after Passover.

08.note: Rav Safra was leaving the Land of Israel for the Diaspora carrying a jug of Sabbatical Year wine, and Rav Huna son of Rav Ika and Rav Kahana went with him. He asked whether anyone had heard how Rabbi Abbahu ruled on whether such produce must be taken back to the Land of Israel. Rav Kahana said Rabbi Abbahu ruled that it must; Rav Huna son of Rav Ika said Rabbi Abbahu ruled that it need not. Rav Safra chose to rely on Rav Huna as a precise transmitter of his teacher's words, like Rahava of Pumbedita. Rav Yosef mocked him with a verse from Hosea, reading it as: whoever is lenient is the one he listens to.
08.why: The Gemara has just cited a dispute over whether Sabbatical Year produce taken abroad must be brought back to the Land of Israel to be removed; this story shows Sages facing that very question on the road and disagreeing over the ruling.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Sage leaving the Land of Israel with Sabbatical Year wine, who asked how to rule.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Ika
people.about: Accompanied Rav Safra and reported a lenient ruling from Rabbi Abbahu.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Accompanied Rav Safra and reported a strict ruling from Rabbi Abbahu.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Mocked Rav Safra for following the lenient report.

people.name: Rahava
people.about: A Sage of Pumbedita known for repeating his teacher's exact words; Rav Safra compared Rav Huna to him.

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when the land of Israel rests; its produce is holy and must be used in set ways.
When a crop is no longer available in the fields, people must clear out the Sabbatical Year produce of that kind still stored in their homes.
Jewish law, or the binding ruling on a particular question.

09.note: Rabbi Yosei relates that Theodosius of Rome led the Jews of Rome to eat young goats roasted whole on the nights of Passover, the way the Passover lamb was prepared in the Temple. The Sages sent him a message: if you were not Theodosius, we would have decreed ostracism on you, for you are close to feeding Israel consecrated food outside the Temple. The Gemara then concludes that a goat roasted whole is forbidden whether or not one calls it Passover meat, while other meat is forbidden only if one says it is for Passover.
09.why: Rav had forbidden saying "this meat is for Passover", since it looks like consecrating a sacrifice; the Gemara raises the Theodosius incident as an objection, because the Sages' message seems to object only to meat roasted whole.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who reports the Theodosius incident.

people.name: Theodosius of Rome
people.about: A leader of the Jews of Rome who had them eat whole roasted goats on Passover night.

terms.meaning: Meat of a sacrifice, which may be eaten only in and around the Temple in Jerusalem.
A ban imposed by the Sages: the person is shunned by the community until the ban is lifted.
Roasted in one piece with its legs and innards, as the Passover lamb was roasted in Temple times.

10.note: Bohayan's son left the corner of his vegetable garden for the poor. His father came and found poor people loaded with vegetables standing at the garden gate. He told them: my sons, throw down what you are carrying, and I will give you twice as much in produce that has been tithed. It is not because I begrudge you, he said, but because the Sages say one does not leave a corner of vegetables for the poor.
10.why: The Gemara has been discussing which vegetables were once given as the corner of the field, a gift owed only on crops that are stored; this story shows a father undoing the gift because vegetables are not subject to it.

people.name: Bohayan
people.about: The father who found the poor carrying his garden's vegetables and offered them tithed produce instead.

people.name: Bohayan's son
people.about: Left the corner of the vegetable garden for the poor.

terms.meaning: The Torah requires a farmer to leave the edge of his field unharvested for the poor; the Sages applied it only to certain crops.
Produce from which the required portions for priests, Levites and others have been set aside, so it may be eaten. A true corner gift is exempt from tithes; vegetables taken as one are not.

11.note: In the Temple, the hides of the most sacred offerings, which belonged to the priests, were at first kept in the Parva chamber and handed out each evening to the priestly family serving that day, but the strongmen among the priests took them by force. The Sages ruled that they be shared out every Friday, when all the priestly watches were present together, yet the prominent priests still seized them. So the owners of the offerings consecrated the hides to Heaven. Within a few days, the Sages said, the whole sanctuary was plated with golden tablets, which were set out on the Temple Mount at the festivals so pilgrims could see the flawless work.
11.why: The Gemara has been discussing the people of Jericho, whose property powerful men took by force; this account of priests seizing hides is a parallel case, followed by Abba Shaul's report of the Jericho owners consecrating their trees for the same reason.

terms.meaning: A room in the Temple courtyard where hides of sacrificed animals were kept.
The priests were divided into groups that took turns serving in the Temple a week at a time; on Friday the outgoing and incoming groups were both present.
Donated to the Temple treasury, so no one could take them for private use.
On the three festivals of Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, Jews came up to Jerusalem to visit the Temple.

12.note: A king and queen were arguing over whether goat or lamb is the better meat, and summoned the High Priest, Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai, to settle it. He waved his hand with contempt and said: if goat were better, let it be brought as the daily offering, which is a lamb. The king said that since he had no reverence for the monarchy, his right hand should be cut off. Yissakhar paid a bribe and his left hand was cut off instead; when the king heard, he had the right hand cut off too. Rav Yosef said: blessed is God who made him pay for his deeds in this world.
12.why: The people in the Temple courtyard had cried out against Yissakhar for wrapping his hands in silk to do the Temple service; the Gemara asks what finally became of him, and this is the answer.

people.name: Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai
people.about: A High Priest who wrapped his hands in silk to do the service, and answered the king with contempt.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who blessed God for punishing Yissakhar in this world.

terms.meaning: A lamb sacrificed in the Temple every morning and every afternoon.
The chief priest of the Temple, who could take a share of any sacrifice.

12.flag: The STORY segment begins mid-story with 'he signaled'; the question from the king and queen that opens it sits in the preceding BEFORE segment.

13.note: Rabbi Simlai came to Rabbi Yohanan and asked him to teach him the Book of Genealogies. Rabbi Yohanan asked where he was from and where he lived; on hearing Lod and Neharde'a, he said that this subject is taught to people of neither place, let alone to someone from both. Rabbi Simlai pressed him until he agreed, then asked to learn it in three months. Rabbi Yohanan threw a clod of earth at him: Berurya, wife of Rabbi Meir, learned three hundred laws a day from three hundred Sages and still could not finish it in three years. As Rabbi Simlai was leaving, he asked a sharp question about the Passover offering, and Rabbi Yohanan, seeing he was a Torah scholar, answered it.
13.why: The mishna rules that a Passover offering slaughtered partly for another purpose is disqualified, but not one slaughtered partly for people who cannot eat it; the question Rabbi Simlai asks on his way out is exactly why the two differ, and Rabbi Yohanan's answer explains it.

people.name: Rabbi Simlai
people.about: A scholar from Lod living in Neharde'a who asked Rabbi Yohanan to teach him the Book of Genealogies.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who refused, relented, threw a clod at Rabbi Simlai, and finally answered his question.

people.name: Berurya
people.about: Wife of Rabbi Meir and daughter of Rabbi Hananya ben Teradyon; Rabbi Yohanan cites her great learning.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Berurya's husband.

people.name: Rabbi Hananya ben Teradyon
people.about: Berurya's father.

terms.meaning: A body of early teachings on the family lists in the biblical book of Chronicles, described here as long and difficult.

terms.term: for its own purpose and for a different purpose
terms.meaning: Slaughtering a Passover offering while intending it, at least partly, as a different kind of sacrifice, which disqualifies it.

terms.term: for those who can eat it and for those who cannot
terms.meaning: Slaughtering the offering for a group that includes people not allowed to eat it, such as the ritually impure; this does not disqualify it.

14.note: King Agrippa once wanted to know how many Jews there were, and told the High Priest to count the Passover lambs. The High Priest took a kidney from each animal, and six hundred thousand pairs of kidneys were found, twice the number who left Egypt. That did not include those who were ritually impure or far away, and no lamb was shared by fewer than ten people. That Passover was called the Passover of the crowded.
14.why: The Gemara has been discussing how crowded the Temple courtyard became on Passover eve, including the one year an old man was crushed; this census shows how vast the crowds could be.

people.name: King Agrippa
people.about: The king who wanted to count the Jewish people and had the Passover lambs counted.

terms.meaning: The Passover offering, a lamb or young goat slaughtered at the Temple on the eve of Passover and eaten that night by a registered group.
In a state, such as after contact with a dead body, that barred a person from the Temple and from eating sacrifices.
The chief priest of the Temple.

15.note: One year the eve of Passover fell on Shabbat, and the sons of Beteira, the leaders of the time, had forgotten whether the Passover offering may be slaughtered on Shabbat. They sent for Hillel, a man from Babylonia who had served the great scholars Shemaya and Avtalyon, and he proved from the Torah that it may. At once they made him Nasi, and he taught the laws of Passover all day, rebuking them for being too lazy to serve Shemaya and Avtalyon. Then they asked what to do if someone forgot to bring his knife before Shabbat. Hillel said he had heard the law and forgotten it, but the people, if not prophets, are sons of prophets. The next day they carried the knives stuck in the lambs' wool or between the goats' horns, and Hillel remembered that this was what he had been taught.
15.why: The mishna has just recorded Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva arguing over which tasks for the Passover offering override Shabbat; the Gemara opens its discussion with this account of how the basic rule, that the slaughter itself overrides Shabbat, was recovered.

people.name: Hillel the Babylonian
people.about: A man from Babylonia who had served Shemaya and Avtalyon; he settled the question and was made Nasi.

people.name: the sons of Beteira
people.about: The leaders of the generation, who had forgotten whether the Passover offering overrides Shabbat.

people.name: Shemaya
people.about: One of the two greatest scholars of the generation, Hillel's teacher.

people.name: Avtalyon
people.about: One of the two greatest scholars of the generation, Hillel's teacher.

terms.meaning: The president, the head of the Sages and of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.
Is performed even on the Sabbath, although the work involved would normally be forbidden that day.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if the rule holds for the lesser thing, it surely holds for the greater.
A punishment from Heaven, being cut off from one's people, for certain grave sins, including failing to bring the Passover offering.

16.note: Yehuda ben Dortai and his son Dortai broke away from the other Sages and went to live in the south. He said: if Elijah comes and asks the Jewish people why they did not bring the Festival peace-offering on Shabbat, what will they answer him? I am astonished at Shemaya and Avtalyon, the two greatest Sages and expounders of the generation, that they did not tell the people that the Festival peace-offering overrides Shabbat.
16.why: The Gemara has been discussing the Festival peace-offering brought on Passover eve alongside the Passover lamb; Yehuda ben Dortai's protest is the dissenting view that it too overrides Shabbat, and Rav then finds his source in a verse.

people.name: Yehuda ben Dortai
people.about: A man who broke away from the Sages over whether the Festival peace-offering overrides Shabbat.

people.name: Dortai
people.about: Yehuda ben Dortai's son, who left with him.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who Jewish tradition says will return; Yehuda imagines him questioning the people.

people.name: Shemaya
people.about: One of the two greatest Sages of the generation, whom Yehuda ben Dortai criticizes.

people.name: Avtalyon
people.about: One of the two greatest Sages of the generation, whom Yehuda ben Dortai criticizes.

terms.meaning: An extra sacrifice brought on Passover eve along with the Passover lamb, so that there would be enough meat for everyone at the meal.
Is offered even on the Sabbath, although the work involved would normally be forbidden that day.

17.note: Rabbi Tarfon did not come to the study hall one evening. The next morning Rabban Gamliel found him and asked why. Rabbi Tarfon said he had been performing the sacred service. Rabban Gamliel said that all his words were astonishing: where is there sacred service nowadays, with the Temple gone? Rabbi Tarfon quoted a verse in which God gives the priests their priesthood "as a service of gift", showing that eating teruma outside the Temple counts as Temple service.
17.why: The Gemara has just argued that eating teruma counts as sacred service, so God accepts it even from a priest later found unfit; it then asks where teruma is called service, and this incident is the source.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A priest and Sage who missed the study hall because he was eating teruma, which he called sacred service.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who asked Rabbi Tarfon why he had not come to the study hall.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to the priests, holy food that only a priest in a state of purity may eat.
The house of study where the Sages met to learn and debate Torah.

18.note: Rabbi Tzadok reports that Rabban Gamliel once told his slave Tavi: go and roast the Passover lamb for us on the perforated grill. The text does not say more about the occasion.
18.why: The mishna forbids roasting the Passover lamb on a grill, then cites this incident, which seems to contradict it; the Gemara explains that a line is missing: a grill with holes, which lets the fire reach the meat, is permitted, and the incident illustrates that.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Told his slave to roast the Passover lamb on a perforated grill.

people.name: Tavi
people.about: Rabban Gamliel's slave.

terms.meaning: The Passover offering, which the Torah requires to be roasted in fire and eaten on Passover night.
A grill full of holes, so the meat is roasted by the fire itself rather than by the heat of the metal.

19.note: Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Avin to take a challenge to Rabbi Abbahu: Rabbi Yohanan seems to judge soft sinews by their present state, yet he told Reish Lakish that the soft hide on a young calf's head is judged by what it will become. When Rabbi Avin put this to him, Rabbi Abbahu said that whoever asked it had not thought it through: Rabbi Yohanan had changed his mind and come over to Reish Lakish's view, telling him, "Do not trouble me", since the source he had relied on was a lone opinion.
19.why: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish have just disagreed over whether people can register for a share of the Passover lamb's sinews that will later harden; this exchange shows that Rabbi Yohanan later retracted and accepted Reish Lakish's view that things are judged by their final state.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Sent a challenge about Rabbi Yohanan's rulings to Rabbi Abbahu.

people.name: Rabbi Avin
people.about: Carried Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Abbahu.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Answered that Rabbi Yohanan had retracted his view.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage whose two rulings seemed to clash; he changed his mind in favor of Reish Lakish.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan's colleague, who asked him about the calf's hide and whose view Rabbi Yohanan came to accept.

terms.meaning: Sign up in advance as one of the group that will eat a particular Passover lamb; one must register for a share of edible meat.
Food can contract ritual impurity, but things that are not food, like hide, cannot; so the question is whether the soft hide counts as food.

20.note: Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan, visited the house of Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak. Asked his name, he said "Rav Huna", using his own title. Invited to sit on the couch, he sat at once; offered a cup of wine, he took it the first time, drank it in two sips, and did not turn his face away. His surprised hosts asked why he called himself Rav Huna, and he said that was the name he was known by. Asked why he sat at once, he said one should do whatever the master of the house says, except if he tells you to leave. The hosts then went on to question the rest of his conduct.
20.why: The mishna says that a bride at the Passover meal turns her face away while eating, out of embarrassment; this visit leads to Rav Huna's answer that only a bride turns her face, not anyone else.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan
people.about: A visitor whose behavior at his hosts' table surprised them, and who explained each thing he did.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: The Sage at whose house Rav Huna was a guest.

terms.meaning: A title for a Sage, like "Rabbi"; calling oneself by it could look conceited.
The host.

20.flag: The STORY segments stop mid-conversation: his answers about the cup, the two sips and not turning his face are in the following AFTER segment.
